path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-01 - Separation choices and continuous contacting.md
gap: Read the operating and equilibrium lines as answers to two different questions. The operating line asks where transferred solute must go to conserve material. The equilibrium line asks which two leaving compositions can coexist without further net transfer. Neither relation supplies a rate. In continuous contact, the gap between them supplies the local driving force; the equipment must supply enough area for finite transfer across that gap.

edits.new:
Read the operating and equilibrium lines as answers to two different questions. The operating line asks where transferred solute must go to conserve material. The equilibrium line asks which two leaving compositions can coexist without further net transfer. Neither relation supplies a rate. In continuous contact, the gap between them supplies the local driving force; the equipment must supply enough area for finite transfer across that gap.

A better solvent can increase that gap, whereas better contacting can increase transfer at the same gap. These improvements act on different parts of the design. Once the fluid has reached its equilibrium limit, increasing turbulence alone cannot make it cross that limit; changing solvent, temperature or pressure changes the limit itself.

## Motivation and explanation

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-02 - Absorption-column equipment.md
gap: Follow a gas parcel through each device. Packing presents a succession of liquid films and renewed interfaces along its path. A tray bubbles the gas through a locally retained liquid pool before the gas advances to the next tray. Both need an interface and a route for the other phase to leave. A support, distributor, weir or downcomer therefore helps establish the flow pattern on which the separation model depends; it is not an accessory that can be omitted after calculating area.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-03 - Gas–liquid equilibrium conventions.md
gap: The density factors are a change of coordinates, not an extra equilibrium effect. At unchanged physical equilibrium, multiply each mole fraction by its phase's total molar density to recover the two concentrations. Substitution then guarantees that all four Henry conventions predict the same pair of physical states. Checking that pair is more informative than comparing the numerical constants in isolation.

The reason is that the same solute partial pressure becomes a smaller fraction of a higher total pressure. State the composition basis before interpreting a pressure effect as changed molecular affinity.

## Motivation and explanation

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-04 - Operating lines and pinch limits.md
gap: The liquid flow changes how quickly solvent becomes loaded as solute is removed from the gas. For fixed gas removal, more solvent shares the transferred solute over more liquid, lowering its outlet concentration. The equilibrium gas concentration over that liquid is then lower, preserving a larger absorption driving force. This is why solvent flow affects height even though the total solute-removal duty is already fixed by the gas specifications.

The minimum is therefore a feasibility boundary approached by increasingly large equipment, not an economical operating point obtained merely by solving the overall balance.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-05 - Two-film resistances and overall coefficients.md
gap: The electrical-resistance analogy concerns a common flux and additive driving-force drops. The two physical concentration drops cannot be added directly because they belong to different phases. Multiplying the liquid drop by the partition coefficient expresses its consequence on the gas basis; only then do the interfacial terms cancel. The analogy does not require gas and liquid concentrations to be continuous at the interface.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-06 - Film models and coefficient measurement.md
gap: The inferred film thickness is the diffusion distance that would reproduce the measured resistance under this model. Keeping that distance fixed while changing solute leaves diffusivity as the only changing factor in $k=D/\delta$, explaining the proportional extrapolation. A different diffusivity exponent in another model represents a different account of exposure and renewal, rather than a unit conversion error.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-07 - Packed-column height and transfer units.md
gap: Rearranging the slice balance for $dz$ asks how much additional height is needed to remove a specified small composition increment. The required height is inversely proportional to the local driving force: a narrow gap costs more height for the same decrement in gas composition. Integrating adds those unequal costs rather than assuming that every part of the bed works at its inlet rate.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-08 - Evaluating NTU and logarithmic driving forces.md
gap: The logarithm comes from integrating the reciprocal of a linearly changing driving force. A small-force end is expensive because the reciprocal weights it strongly, so an arithmetic average of the endpoint forces gives too much credit to the favourable end. The log mean packages that exact integral into one effective force for the linear case; it is not a preferred average chosen independently of the balance.

The apparent zero divided by zero is a feature of the logarithmic expression, so taking its limit must recover the ordinary composition change divided by that common force. Curved equilibrium requires the actual intervening profile, not just this endpoint check.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-09 - HETP and theoretical-stage relationships.md
gap: One ideal stage imposes equilibrium on leaving streams, which converts the gap from one stage to the next by a multiplicative factor. Continuous contacting instead integrates a local rate over a continuously varying gap. The logarithm of the stage factor and the continuous driving-force integral therefore produce different dimensionless counts even for the same specified separation.

In the worked example, both routes predict the same packed height after each count is multiplied by its own appropriate height measure. The disagreement between the counts is consequently not a conservation error. Using NTU as a tray count would combine the count from one model with the length scale from another.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-10 - Packed-column hydraulics and diameter.md
gap: At fixed total gas flow, reducing cross-section increases superficial velocity and hence the gas's opposition to liquid drainage. Greater liquid holdup then narrows the remaining gas passages, which raises resistance further. This feedback explains the sharp upward turn near flooding: a low-loading pressure-drop power law cannot represent a geometry that is progressively filling with liquid.

The velocity fraction must be squared because the chart ordinate depends on gas mass flux squared. This is an algebraic consequence of the chosen ordinate, not a different flooding margin. After selecting diameter, the new gas and liquid flows per unit area must also be used in the mass-transfer calculation; diameter and height are coupled through hydrodynamics.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/01 - Introduction and absorption/SEP-11 - Designing an ammonia absorber.md
gap: The calculation deliberately uses equilibrium twice for different purposes. First, equilibrium with the entering gas defines a limiting liquid loading and hence a minimum solvent flow. After selecting an actual flow, the operating balance supplies the actual liquid loading at each location. Only then does equilibrium supply the hypothetical gas counterpart used to calculate the local driving force. Substituting the pinch loading as the actual outlet would undo the chosen margin above minimum flow.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-12 - Drying equipment and wet solids.md
gap: Dry-basis accounting removes a moving denominator. Evaporating liquid changes the wet product mass, so a decrease in wet-basis moisture combines a change of liquid inventory with a change in the reference mass. Dividing by the conserved dry solid isolates the inventory that is actually being removed. This is why the dry-basis moisture difference can be multiplied directly by dry-solid mass.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-13 - Humidity and saturation charts.md
gap: At fixed pressure and humidity, the vapour-to-carrier mole ratio and thus vapour partial pressure stay fixed during sensible heating. Saturation pressure rises with temperature, so relative humidity falls even though no water has left the gas. The gas becomes more capable of accepting water because its equilibrium endpoint has moved, not because heating has reduced its existing vapour inventory.

Percentage saturation uses a mass ratio with dry gas as denominator; relative humidity uses a partial-pressure ratio. The nonlinear conversion between mass ratio and partial pressure explains their unequal numerical values away from the dilute-vapour limit. Both locate the same physical state when their definitions are used consistently.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-14 - Humid enthalpy and adiabatic saturation.md
gap: Per kilogram of dry gas, evaporation increases the latent contribution to gas enthalpy while reducing its sensible-temperature contribution. A falling temperature can therefore accompany an almost unchanged total enthalpy. The word adiabatic refers to heat crossing the chosen boundary; the inlet hot gas already brings energy and the added liquid brings its own enthalpy.

This is why guessing an outlet saturation temperature and reading its humidity is insufficient: the guessed state may demand energy that the incoming streams do not supply.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-15 - Dew point and cooling moist gas.md
gap: Dew point is an endpoint determined by the vapour already present. Two unsaturated gas samples at different initial temperatures but the same humidity and pressure have the same dew point; they need different sensible-cooling duties to reach it. Increasing their initial temperature changes that duty without changing the first-condensation condition.

edits.old: This condition is independent of the initial gas temperature as long as that temperature is above the dew point. Temperature establishes how much cooling is needed; $H$ and $P$ establish where condensation starts.

Once condensation starts, further cooling removes vapour as well as energy, so the fixed-humidity construction must stop. A downstream equilibrium cooler calculation follows the saturation boundary and includes the condensed-liquid stream. This change in the mass balance is the reason the pre-condensation path cannot simply be extended below dew point.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-16 - Wet bulb and simultaneous heat and mass transfer.md
gap: The surface temperature is selected by competing rates. If it falls, the temperature difference supplying heat grows, while its saturation humidity falls and reduces evaporation demand. If it rises, the opposite changes occur. Their intersection fixes the steady wet-bulb temperature; it is not the saturation temperature of the unchanged bulk humidity.

If it rises, the opposite changes occur. Their intersection fixes the steady wet-bulb temperature; it is not the saturation temperature of the unchanged bulk humidity.

Adiabatic saturation is instead an overall stream-energy and equilibrium construction. The two temperatures are close for air/water because the relevant heat and mass transport properties approximately match, not because every wet surface must reproduce an ideal saturator. The chloroform example makes the limit of that analogy visible.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-17 - Equilibrium moisture and drying periods.md
gap: Critical moisture marks a mismatch of rates: internal liquid supply can no longer support the evaporation demanded by the gas at a fully wet surface. Raising external demand can cause that mismatch earlier even in unchanged material. Equilibrium moisture answers a different question: how much liquid remains when there is no net thermodynamic driving force under the specified gas conditions.

Its temperature rise is therefore part of the mechanism indicating that the wet-surface model is losing validity. Continuing the constant-rate division into this region would assume away the very internal limitation that defines it.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-18 - Countercurrent drying and minimum gas flow.md
gap: The minimum gas ratio follows from water-carrying capacity, while the actual ratio sets the local humidity rise per unit water picked up. With more dry gas, each increment of evaporated water causes a smaller humidity increase, leaving the gas farther from saturation. The selected margin therefore creates a finite driving force but does not by itself determine residence time.

In countercurrent operation, plot position along the solid path and position along the gas path run in opposite directions. Anchoring the operating line at the dry-solid/fresh-gas end fixes that pairing before any signs are chosen. The negative driving-force slope is a consequence of this physical pairing, not a convention that can be copied unchanged to cocurrent operation.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-19 - Analytical drying times across two regimes.md
gap: The operative drying rate is the smaller of the externally supported wet-surface rate and the material's fitted internal-supply rate. At the crossing, both descriptions predict the same rate, so the time calculation changes branch continuously. An algebraic crossing outside the specified moisture interval does not belong to the trajectory and cannot justify adding a second time contribution.

Near the fitted equilibrium endpoint, internal moisture removal becomes slow even with favourable gas. Their separate denominators show why eliminating one limitation need not eliminate the other.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-20 - Cocurrent drying and flow arrangement.md
gap: In the specified cocurrent case the external rate stays below the fitted internal-supply rate throughout the target interval, so a wet surface can be maintained down to the chosen endpoint. Countercurrent operation assigns different gas conditions to the same solid moisture and therefore crosses the two rates at a different point. The change in calculated regimes follows from matching local demand to local supply, not from a change in the material coefficients.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-21 - Graphical calculation of drying time.md
gap: The rate family supplies the material response at a specified pair of moisture and gas driving force; the operating line selects the sequence of those pairs that this dryer actually visits. Reading all rates from one fixed-humidity curve would model a different experiment. The graphical construction is a substitution of the conservation path into the measured rate law before integration.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/02 - Drying of solids/SEP-22 - Other solvents and nonadiabatic drying.md
gap: Adding surface heat changes both sides of the local balance. Some additional energy supports faster evaporation; some is offset by a reduced gas-to-surface temperature difference as the surface warms. Assigning all added power to extra latent heat would incorrectly hold the surface temperature and saturation humidity fixed. Assigning it all to warming would incorrectly hold evaporation fixed.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/03 - Membrane separations/SEP-23 - Membrane mechanisms and structure.md
gap: The product $D_jH_j$ combines two successive requirements: the species must enter the material and then move through it. Strong sorption increases the amount available inside the membrane to establish a gradient; high diffusivity converts that gradient into rapid transport. Comparing only molecular size misses the sorption contribution, while comparing only affinity misses mobility.

Making an ideal selective layer thinner multiplies both species' permeances by the same thickness factor, leaving their ideal selectivity unchanged. It improves throughput without automatically improving composition discrimination. Defects and support resistance can break this ideal scaling, which is why a thin material film still needs module-level verification.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/03 - Membrane separations/SEP-24 - Membrane modules and operating modes.md
gap: Recycle changes how often liquid passes the membrane, while net recovery measures how much fresh feed ultimately leaves as permeate. They answer different questions because the recycle crosses only an internal process boundary. A large circulating flow can sustain useful wall shear even when net feed and product rates are modest.

A change in the bulk-based rejection can therefore reflect a changed boundary layer as well as a changed selective layer.

path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/03 - Membrane separations/SEP-26 - Binary gas membrane selectivity.md
gap: The local composition appears in its own driving force: enriching the emerging permeate raises the permeate partial pressure of the preferred gas, reducing the pressure difference that caused that enrichment. Solving the quadratic makes this feedback self-consistent. Choosing a root is therefore a physical check of mole fractions and flux directions, not just an algebraic preference for the smaller numerical root.

The downstream example remains enriched relative to its local retentate while being poorer than the original feed. path: other/obsidian/CEBT-II Notes/Separations II/03 - Membrane separations/SEP-27 - Estimating gas membrane area.md
gap: There are two averages to establish, with different weights. Collected permeate composition is weighted by how much gas each patch produces. The area calculation is weighted by how much area is needed to transfer each increment at its local flux. Replacing both by endpoint arithmetic means imposes two separate approximations, so correcting the flux average alone cannot make the whole calculation exact.

The reference-volume convention allows the total-flow and oxygen-flow balances to share the same amount basis. Compression changes the operating volume of that gas, but not its number of moles. Omitting the second term would treat the membrane like a dilute absorber with constant total gas flow, although a substantial fraction of the whole gas stream is being removed.
